MISS JANE WOOD.

On January 6 last you published the portrait of our client, Miss Jane Wood, on a half-page advertisement of Sandow's corsets. Miss Wood desires it to be known that she gave no permission for, and was in no way a party to, the publication of her name or portrait in connection with the Sandow corset. She has, in fact, never worn Sandow corsets.

The unwarranted use which has been made of her photograph has caused great annoyance to her and her relatives and friends, and is, moreover, calculated to mislead the public. Miss Wood has commenced an action against the parties responsible. Herbert Reeves and Co.

[The advertisement was received by our advertisement department in the ordinary way of business, and we had no reason to suspect that the publication of the portrait of Miss Jane Wood, a well-known actress, was unauthorised. We, however, desire to express to Miss Jane Wood our regret for the improper use that was made of her portrait in our columns.—EDITOR.]

"Once begin, and you must go on: therefore, don't begin"—it is the way they have of frightening people from moderate rectifications, by showing them immoderate revolutions.

Thus, when it is claimed that a man or a woman should not be bound for life—a life, as it generally happens, of immorality—to a raving lunatic, it is answered: "Oh, but if you begin to divorce for lunacy, you must go on. You must divorce for leprosy. Then you must divorce for influenza. Soon you will be divorced for a cold. For there is no doubt that a person with a very bad cold looks extremely plain and is in every way an unpleasant companion. It is good that people should be bound to maniacs, in case other people should claim colds as an excuse for escaping from their wives." Such, slightly caricatured, is our old friend, the thin-end-of-the-wedge argument.

When it fails to carry very strong conviction, another argument, not unlike it, is added. This is the argument from some extraordinary single set of circumstances, some strange event, that happened somewhere, or was said by someone now dead to have happened somewhere else; and is in every way so amazing and unusual that (the argument concludes) it will immediately happen again

BIRKBECK BANK
PAYS OUT MONEY.
FOUR MILLIONS PROVIDED

The Birkbeck Bank opened its doors at 10 a.m. yesterday to make the first payment of ten shillings in the £ to its depositors, and all day long until 4 p.m. the business of paying out money went on. It will be resumed at 10 a.m. to-day.
Four millions had been provided for this purpose by the Bank of England—about half a million in gold and silver and the rest in notes.

The first of what was ultimately to be a long queue of depositors arrived at the bank's doors at 8.30 p.m. on Sunday; at midnight there were about a dozen waiting, and at 10 a.m., when the first batch of about twenty-five was admitted, the queue numbered about 300, growing steadily until the bank closed at 4 p.m.
But during the day it was only possible to attend to some 350 of a total of perhaps 2,000 who waited at one time or another outside.

Towards closing time the crowd made a rush as a batch was being admitted, but the strong force of police soon restored order.

The present payment does not affect "A" and "B" shareholders, whose claims will be dealt with later.
WAIT IN EARLY MORNING.
In the early hours of yesterday an anxious group of men and women stood waiting outside the Birkbeck Bank.
These depositors, who in many cases urgently needed money to pay off various bills and rates, brought bags of sandwiches and biscuits with them.
By 6 a.m., some thirty depositors were waiting, and by 10 a.m., a queue of over 300 people had formed. Many of them had travelled long distances to get to the bank.
In the queue were clergymen, girl typists, commissionaires, young City clerks and old men by the score.
Many of the people in the queue fainted during the day owing to exhaustion, while two cases were so serious that they had to be treated at the King's College Hospital.

At twenty minutes to four—the banking chamber being then full—the cordon of police, numbering quite 100 men, broke up the waiting queue outside the Birkbeck Bank, saying that enough depositors were inside already to keep the tellers busy till closing time at four o'clock.
THIS WEDDING DAY.

Quietly and with many words of consolation the police moved the disappointed people away. A number of depositors protested, chiefly old ladies, who could not understand why such important business as paving out should cease so early.

There was, however, one exception—a white-haired old lady, who leaned on the arm of her daughter, who was herself advanced in years. "My poor head is aching so," she said, "that I am glad to go. I live in Blackfriars, and this is the first time I've been across the river for twenty years."
Two sad cases were related. A typical middle-aged business man told how he had been admitted to a junior partnership with his firm after twenty-five years' loyal work.
"The first money I drew as a partner," he said, "a sum of £200, I paid into the Birkbeck on the morning of the very day it closed. It was the first time I ever had £200 all at once."

4,000-MILE TRIP TO VISIT
SIR HIRAM MAXIM.
A small boy with a popgun and an armful of toys has just crossed America and the Atlantic, all by himself, for a visit to London.
The small boy who so cheerfully undertook a 4,000-mile journey alone was Master E. Maxim Joubert, the seven-year-old grandson of Sir Hiram Maxim, the inventor of the famous gun.
Master Joubert came from Boston, U.S.A., to visit his grandparents at their home at "Rye Cote," Dulwich Common, where he has arrived safely after his Transatlantic adventures.
"He is a clever boy," said Sir Hiram Maxim to an "Express" representative last night, while Master E. Maxim Joubert, fresh from his travels, played with toy guns and soldiers.
"He travelled from his home in Boston to New York, and as no one of the family could cross with him, he came over on the Cunard liner Lusitania alone.
"I hear he made himself quite at home and happy on board, and occupied cabin B 71 in solitary state, and was no trouble to the captain or the stewardess on the way."
"“Lady Maxim met him at Liverpool, and showed him the way back to our home at Dulwich Common. He is quite pleased with what he has seen of England.”

Little Maxim Joubert was the most popular passenger on the Lusitania on the voyage. He waved his hand in adieu to his American friends as the vessel backed out from the landing stage, and then took command of the ship.
He was much petted by the lady passengers on board, and told them all about guns and battles and adventures with pirates, in which he himself was chiefly concerned.

London Hospital Doctor Discusses His Remarkable Complaint.
The bridle man, Allan Rushbrook, is apparently none the worse for his long journey from Swainsthorpe, Norfolk, to the London Hospital.
Great interest has been aroused in the medical profession by the curious nature of his illness, and his case is being closely watched.

An examination by the house doctor today showed that almost all the surface muscles of Rushbrock's body have turned into bone. The only parts at present in which he has the power of movement are the upper part of the left arm and the lower jaw.
Such a case was previously unheard of," an Evening News representative was told at the hospital to-day.

"There have been cases where parts of the body have been affected in this way. Among rough riders the flesh above the knee sometimes turns to bone. Mental shock will occasionally produce the same effect in other parts.
"But for the whole body to be thus affected was unknown."
"There is no known cure, because few opportunities have been given for studying the disease. The process is understood, but we cannot explain its cause."

How to Derive the Most Benefit from Sea Bathing.
(By a Trained Teacher of Physical Culture.) This week I am giving some exercises which everyone should do, but which are especially good for people who are troubled with a bad circulation.

Now, it may seem a little out of place to talk about a bad circulation with the thermometer where it is at present, but strangely enough people whose blood does not circulate freely suffer—more than those whose circulation is normal—from extremes of heat as well as cold.

A good circulation as a rule means freedom from winter ailments, such as coughs, colds and chilblains, and all-the-year-round complaints like indigestion and kindred ills. It also prevents nervous troubles and brain fag, and from a beauty point of view it means a clear, beautiful skin and bright, thick hair.
It will be seen how important it is not to wait till winter before going in for physical culture.

Stand bending slightly forwards, shoot out first the left, then the right arm, and pull it back sharply as far as ever it will go. Continue to do this very briskly, bending lower and lower till the ground is reached, then gradually rise again, still shooting out the arms as you do so.
